title: Simridhi Makhija on Content Creation, Networking, and Modern Dating
summary: Content creator Simridhi Makhija discusses her journey from Delhi debating societies to creating viral content and building Speakfest in Bangalore. She argues that immediate execution, authenticity, and opinionated communication outperform rigid algorithm strategies and corporate expectations.
key_points: Embrace 'Serendipity-Maxing': Being in startup-dense hubs like Bangalore and putting in minimal social effort allows founders and creators to naturally cross paths with investors and collaborators in everyday settings like cafes.

Practice 'Retard-Maxing' over strategic overthinking: Rather than over-optimizing camera quality, ideal posting times, or elaborate hooks, focus on rapid execution and publishing raw thoughts consistently.

Content succeeds through authentic truth: Replicating competitors or reverse-engineering algorithms leads to generic content; audiences resonate with raw, genuine disclosures about one's real life and industry realities.

Specific niches attract broader audiences: Highly specific perspectives (e.g., the dating observations of a 23-year-old woman in Bangalore or books on male collar styles) generate strong curiosity and engagement across diverse demographics.

Dating teaches core sales and presentation skills: Going on dates forces individuals to learn soft-selling, likability, and emotional connection, which are directly transferable to business development and client pitches.

Work-life balance is unrealistic for aggressive builders: Attempting to build a successful startup in four years instead of fifteen requires intense dedication and emotional investment where conventional boundaries cannot apply.
Master 'Opinionated Framing': When interviewing or presenting, focus on being engaging and memorable through storytelling and distinct viewpoints rather than merely reciting safe, conventional facts.

Adopt an 'Early User Energy': Traditional education systems lag behind rapid technological advancements; professionals must self-educate and experiment proactively with emerging tools like Claude and ChatGPT to avoid obsolescence.
content: Transcript: Host: What actually triggered you to create content after coming to Bangalore? Simridhi Makhija: College was never about political science honours, that was something that I was doing at that time. It was about debating. We used to go to like, three debates a week, and we used to also win all of that, not to brag. Host: Who's Simridhi? Do you happen to come from Delhi to Bangalore because of air quality issue or? Simridhi Makhija: Not for the air quality issue. I think my life quality issue. If you're looking for anonymity enough that you can do your stuff, not Mumbai, not Delhi, like Bangalore is the place. Host: A lot of girls post the dating screenshots of the guys they do or the guys also do vice versa. It should be private. People trust you and text you on the dating apps. Do you think it's actually you should do that or how does it work? Simridhi Makhija: I think you should do that without naming the person. Host: Why people tend to take dating advice from girls rather than boys and they don't trust boys, why? Simridhi Makhija: And Kanye West also says that, that I don't care about what my audience thinks, I just do what I want to do and in that way they like it. Host: What do you think, since you have dated a few people here and you have gone through a lot of networking and people here, also interacted with a lot of content creators, like how can we handle them? Simridhi Makhija: Being a Gen Z myself, I don't like the culture that's going on with the Gen Z, that I am not going to work after 7:00 PM, I'm not going to take the call, I'm going to leave the meeting, and I'm going to tell the boss that you know what, I'm off and you don't get to tell me what to do. I think if you want to reduce that gap, you need to know exactly what you want in life, exactly what you want from a partner, and also have realistic expectations. There are literally girls out there who are asking ChatGPT why their boyfriend did the thing that he did or will the situationship work out. So all our knowledge is coming from LLMs and not real people. Host: So what is the biggest lie the creator economy is telling to younger people? Host: Welcome to Sculptors Podcast. If you are a person who is looking out for dating advice or a playbook, and also a founder who is looking out for creating content, today we have a very interesting person called Simridhi, who has cracked her way towards creating content on Instagram and also she speaks a lot about dating. Welcome, Simridhi. So I think it's been 6 months you have been in Bangalore, right? Simridhi Makhija: Yeah, yeah, 6 months today. Host: So for me as a person from Chennai, I used to occasionally visit for business meetings here. But for a person who is from Delhi, stayed here for 6 months, like what do you think Bangalore has offered you and can you just elaborate on that side? Simridhi Makhija: I love that question. Bangalore to me, and to anybody who comes here, is serendipity-maxing. Now what do I mean by that? I basically mean that this place has so many opportunities. It's a hub spot of so many businesses, so many startups, that anybody who comes here and even puts like a little bit of effort into connecting with people, they will meet the right person in the right place. They don't even have to do a lot. If you just... So I met a founder recently who later became a friend, and he also told me that he didn't even have to go out of his way to meet investors, even if he's just sitting at a cafe and is noticing people there, he's running into these people. So Bangalore to me has been serendipity-maxing, and thankfully my father has taught me skills like hard work and dedication, and I had those plus serendipity-maxing, so it became something that worked. Host: That's very interesting. I had a look at your LinkedIn profile, right? You have been a marketer in the previous years. So is it something which you planned that after coming to Bangalore you have to create content, or what actually triggered you to create content after coming to Bangalore? Simridhi Makhija: That's a great question. So I had always wanted to create reels, like I always knew I want to do it. But when I came to Bangalore, the true story is this, that when I came to Bangalore, I was struggling a lot with the agency bit, then I had some personal stuff that I was going through. So then I was just walking to home one day and I was like, look, I'm already in so much pain, and I also know that I want to start creating reels, so I don't care what my hair looks like, I don't care what my makeup look like. Let's just go. So I just, you know, pulled up my camera and I was like, let's just record, and I put it out there. First reel got 5,000 views, and people were really nice in the comments etc. So I just made a rule that I'm going to post every single day. That's what I did and that's what worked. So to answer your question, I think I always wanted to make reels, but that pain was something that was really the outlet of how it happened. Host: That was very candid, so it was really nice. And another question I want to ask is like, is it very planned that you want to shoot in low quality, because a lot of people have started experimenting after your reels, like once it got viral, a lot of people thought algorithm is eventually pushing low quality content. What do you think? Simridhi Makhija: I wish I were that smart that I could plan everything and plan the low-quality videos. I'm not that smart, you're over-crediting me. It was a happenstance that I had that phone that time. I never really like wanted to change it or whatever, and then like I said, it was coming from so much pain that I didn't even care what my camera quality was. So imagine a situation wherein you are in so much pain already that other types of pain don't even clock. That was my situation. I didn't care about anything. Host: That's interesting. Who's Simridhi, like from a background like where you brought up, how you grow, can you just elaborate on that side? Simridhi Makhija: Sure. So I have done my schooling from Delhi, I have done my college from Delhi. I have always been the nerdiest kid in the class, like and I always wanted to care about more whether I'm in the student council or whether I'm the head girl, and not care about extracurriculars or even developing my personality. Like that was the Simridhi in school. And then I came to college and then I was like, you know, I have always been a studious student, but now there are so many activities. Where do I shine? Like that's the question I asked myself. And then I saw the opening of this debating society, like you can become a part of the debating society. I applied, got into the debating society. But even there, the obsession of, you know, just being in the student council or something was still there. So then I applied to be the president of the debating society, became that. And so college was never about political science honours, that was something that I was doing at that time, it was about debating. Like trust me, we used to go to like three debates a week, and we used to also win all of that, not to brag. But yeah, so that was college. Host: That's why you keep on fighting on Twitter, or how does it work? Simridhi Makhija: Yeah, I deliberately start fires. No, I'm just kidding. Host: A lot of tweets are like a bit controversial at times, right? So I just want to understand. So it's political science that you was pretty much interested, or? Simridhi Makhija: So there was a phase in my life wherein I was like a political junkie. I used to watch the news, I used to tweet political stuff. I've deleted that account, so no use finding that out now. Host: Instagram also is something that you deleted and started new, or is it? Simridhi Makhija: It was only Twitter back then, only Twitter. So I used to do all of that, but there was a point, and this also hurts to say, there was a point wherein I realized that actually it doesn't make sense for me to lose my sleep and react a lot on what's happening in the political realm. So then I shifted more towards my own growth and more towards philosophy instead, because that energy is still there, you still need to make it have an outlet, but then outlet that changed. Because I think, I think a part of wisdom is also realizing that you can't really change politics. Host: There is a lot been happening right now, right? Elections are happening, war is happening on other side. Like a lot of people have told that our human brain doesn't have the capacity to go through a lot of those things. Simridhi Makhija: 100%. Host: So what do you think on that side? Simridhi Makhija: I think 100% human brain is not designed to live the life that we are leading right now. And the thing is, we sit on Instagram all day long and we see those people who have nutritionists, who have physicians, who have personal trainers in the gym, and they look at their lives and their bodies and their lifestyles and think that I am not doing anything in my life. But the thing is that you guys are leading entirely different lives. You can't look at somebody who has every expert in the world, you know, at their doorstep and expect that you too are going to have the same life, and that's exactly what's leading to disaster. You need to realize that biologically, we are designed to only meet 20 people who are in our neighborhood. But now we see somebody who is living in Germany their best life and we think that I'm not doing good enough or I am not good enough. So we are definitely not designed for what's happening in the world. Host: There's a lot of comparison through social lives and Instagram, right? Simridhi Makhija: 100%. Host: Okay, so how you happen to become a marketer from doing college as a debate, something like that, and then how the transition of marketer came in place? Simridhi Makhija: So I feel like serendipity has been a big part of my life now also, and thankfully from college time also. So I remember I didn't sit for placement, by the way. So I remember that when the placement time came around, I didn't sit, so I was worried okay, what's going to happen, this and that. And then one day my friend was coming to meet me and I was sitting in the canteen waiting for him, and randomly I see this opening with the Ministry of Commerce and Industry and they were looking for interns in the social media team. I was like, okay, this looks interesting, and my father always says that working in the government is cool, so let's just try to fill it. Host: Every parent in India thinks so. Simridhi Makhija: Every parent in India thinks so. I was like let's just try to see what's up with this. So then I filled that form, and that was thanks to the 20 minutes my friend was late, because had he come on the right time, I wouldn't have filled it. But then I filled up that form, and guess what? From the Government of India, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry for whom I'd filled this form, they didn't reach out to me for 6 months. Host: Okay. Simridhi Makhija: So I was like okay, this is an opportunity slipped through the crack, let's just forget it. After 6 months, those guys call me up and they're like, hey, do you want to work? And then the interview happened and then got in. Host: Did you thank your friend for that? Simridhi Makhija: No, I forgot. But that happened, and then after I worked with the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, I realized that I have a bend for marketing, I have a bend for connecting with people emotionally, which I think is a big part of marketing. Host: Yes. Simridhi Makhija: So I think that is something that happened. Luck, serendipity, whatever you want to call it. Host: Nice. Do you happen to come from Delhi to Bangalore because of air quality issue or how does it happen? Simridhi Makhija: I mean, not for the air quality issue, but I think my life quality issue. Because I was in Delhi, and like I told you, I had done my schooling and college and everything in Delhi. So I was like, you know, it's time to get out of the Delhi bubble, because unless you see something new, you don't even realize what your faults are, your shortcomings, pardon me, are. So then I said that you know, I'm going to go to Bangalore and I'm going to go to a networking event. And TiE was the networking event that I came to. For 7 days that event was happening, and then it only took me 7 days to fall in love with Bangalore, I guess. Host: I have seen a tweet or a carousel wrote about Bangalore and why people actually choose Bangalore more than the ecosystem and other things. Varun has written this tweet, I think. He told me that as he wrote that mostly people come to Bangalore from different locations so that they don't have that peer of relations and other things, like in Delhi if you are there, you'll have your relatives and other people surrounded. So whatever you do, you'll have a conscious judgment of whether your relatives are seeing or something like that. When you come to a different city, and city like Bangalore has more freedom and people are more welcoming. So do you agree with that tweet or what is your thoughts on that? Simridhi Makhija: I think 100%, like people are more welcoming here. And Bangalore to me is like a global city if you ask me. There are not just people from Bangalore, and obviously from across the country, but also from outside the country. Especially in places like Indiranagar, Koramangala, you see a lot of these people coming in from different countries and that's the kind of exposure you need. But I think there is another side of it which nobody talks about, which is that Bangalore actually is also a city wherein everybody knows everybody. Like within my circle if I talk about, like just the veins of the body are so interconnected that there's going to be some mutual connection who would know. So that way, within the industry everybody knows everybody, but yes, if you're looking for anonymity enough that you can do your stuff, this is the city for you. Like I can bet on my life that not Mumbai, not Delhi, like Bangalore is the place. Host: So I think it's been 6 months you have started creating content. So after creating content, what are the opportunities that opened to you after creating content? Like I think NDTV featured your thing, so what are your thoughts after that creating content? Simridhi Makhija: Tanmay Bhat also says this, that once you start creating content, a lot of the people who see your content might reach out to you, and that's exactly what happened with me. A lot of interesting opportunities opened up. I don't know if you know, but we recently did a live show at Big Pitcher, Indiranagar, which was a talk show, it's that simple. We did it with another influencer. Host: Nice. Simridhi Makhija: And those are the opportunities that I look for, because when you do something like a live show, people actually come in with their real questions and they have real conversations, which is exactly what happened in that live show also. And so when I get to do things like that, it just makes the content creation journey very worth it. So if anybody's listening to this, like just take this from me, that content creation does open a lot of doors, but then you just have to make sure that you are putting the best work out there. Host: A lot of people get confused here. So for them, what is best work that you would suggest? Simridhi Makhija: Best work is truth. So whatever you do, just be very genuine in what you are saying and doing, because what is happening right now is people are trying to reverse engineer success, so they would do something that's working and would try to replicate it, which is exactly why it doesn't work. Host: Okay, so there is no authenticity or originality from them. Simridhi Makhija: Exactly. What they need to do instead is they need to find out what is the most true thing that they can say about their industry, about their life, about what they're going through, and that is something that works. So this whole copying business that's going around, that's never going to work. You have to figure out what is the most genuine thing about your industry. Can you talk about that? Talk about that. Host: I've seen all your reels, but why there is no reel about you, why you exactly started and other things? You didn't have a chance, or are you planning to do it in the future? Simridhi Makhija: Actually, I'm not planning to do this in the future also, because the thing is, I feel like I am not as important as the idea is. So to me, the idea is God, and my duty is to do justice to the idea, which is what I try to do with every reel. But I think I'm not important enough to, you know, be talking about myself. In conversations like this, I'm very happy, but generally, I don't prefer that. Host: Understood. What made you to start creating content on dating? Why does it happen? Simridhi Makhija: I think it's just a blessing of being a girl in your early 20s, because you meet guys and then you have experiences and then you also find truths about life in that journey. And to anybody who's in their 20s and listening to this, I feel like go out there and date, please. It's not a bad thing or it's not taboo. It also teaches you about life. And as one of my very good friends says, that even for guys, when guys go out and they go on dates, they learn more about sales by doing that, instead of sitting with their guy friends and hanging out with them. Because once you are on a date with a woman, you have to basically sell yourself, but in a subtle way, not in a way that's going to put them off. So I think dating is a phenomenal way of learning things about life, about yourself. So go out there and do that. I did that and then you know, I got some truths along the way, and then I talk about them. Host: So in your tweet, I think you have posted that in your 20s, founders don't get into relationship or commitment, right? I'm someone who's more against it is what I feel, because see, when you have a commitment towards a woman or something to hold on, I think you tend to put your heart and soul on something that you build, and also build a life along with her, right? So what made you to write that statement of tweet? Simridhi Makhija: You're right when you say that you would want to put your heart and your commitment for one woman and not care about love life anymore because you're already sorted. But very practically speaking, it doesn't happen. Because the thing is, the founder life requires maniac number of hours, maniac number of hours. So once you, you know, are trying to balance your founder life and your love life, it's very impractical that it will work out. Because I have seen cases of founders wherein they have been married for 2 years, and by the way, like imagine what I'm going to say, they've been married for 2 years and they have met each other for dinner like three times. You can count on their fingers three times. And this is my very close friend, by the way, who's a founder, and without sharing a lot of details, he's divorcing now and he's like, this was my fault and I couldn't, you know, balance etc. So when I look at cases like that, I'm like founders should probably think thrice before they get into something, because their life requires something that is honestly not something that everybody can pull off. Host: Partially I agree. Okay, maybe there may be a case-to-case basis, I think so. A lot of experiences, a lot of people. Okay, so how do you see a content scene in Bangalore? Like do you see a lot of content creators coming up, or how does it? Simridhi Makhija: I think Bangalore has a lot of content creators, which is amazing. I feel like more people need to create content because there is so much untapped potential also. Remember I told you about the talk show that we did? So there were a lot of people who wanted to start creating content and they were just unsure where to start. So I think Bangalore is a prime example of that, because I know people here who are creating content about very niche topics such as male fashion. And I looked at this content creator who was creating about male fashion, and they were talking about how there is a literal book about just male fashion. So imagine how your tie should be. If you have a round face, what kind of collar you should go for. What kind of pants you should go for depending on the ratios of your body. There is a whole book on that, and a guy's creating content on it. So there is so much you can talk about, but on a niche level, and Bangalore people are doing that. To give you another example, there is a friend who's trying to create a clothing brand, but just for vests. So vests you wear inside. But he's like, but women have the options of vest equivalents and they wear it, you know, as almost tops, but men don't have that alternative, so let me create content on that. Host: That's pretty much interesting. Nice. You think that more niche-related content, there is more gap that people can create? Simridhi Makhija: 100%. So the more specific, the better it is, right? So if I talk about my dating experience as a 23-year-old girl in Bangalore, that's super specific, but that talks to people at a lot of levels. Because even somebody who's a 40-year-old woman would be interested in knowing what's happening in the life of a 23-year-old girl, and that's exactly how it works in other niches also. The more specific you can get, the more shock you're also creating in other people about what you're talking about. So you should always ask this question as the first question, that how specific can I get with the content that I'm trying to create. Host: When you had a chance to come across a concept called 'retard-max', which you eventually started doing, and also now we are conducting an event called Speakfest to teach others, right? Can you just give us a thought process on how you happen to come across that? Simridhi Makhija: Okay, so I am more on Twitter than I am on Instagram. So the thing is on Twitter I had always known about this concept called retard-maxing. And then one day I just talked about retard-maxing on my platform. And the concept of retard-maxing is very simple. You do not try to over-optimize your life, and you just do the thing that needs to be done. And what I love about retard-maxing is that retard-maxing is less about planning and it's more about execution. As they say on Twitter, a retard only executes. He doesn't like over-plan or over-strategize, which is something the world has fooled us with. And I get a lot of... I get angry on that also, because a lot of gurus out there telling us when exactly to post, what exactly to post, what should be the hook, etc. Please retard-max and please post it out there. It's going to work better than you just sitting out there and thinking for 2 months as to what you should post. Host: Do you agree that there is a strategy in place and other things which eventually work, or you just think that whatever thoughts you have, if you go and put it out there, it will work? For I think since I feel why it worked for you, my thought was like since you are from a marketing background, since you have the experience of debate, when I just reverse engineer and see what you have done so far, for you maybe that has inherently worked is what I feel. For people that we suggest to do retard-max, maybe they don't have that experience of speaking from the correct pattern, like they don't even know what is storytelling or nothing, right? So will it work for them as well? Simridhi Makhija: So the thing is, it has to be a mix of both. It has to be a mix of strategy, because the thing is you don't want to be a winner who only wins once. You want to be somebody who keeps on winning. And in that paradigm, you obviously need a strategy, so I give points there. But when I talk about retard-maxing, here's the principle behind it. The principle behind it is that even the world doesn't know what it requires. As the Ford founder said that if I asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses, right? So even people don't know what they want. And when you retard-max and you just do things your way, not caring about what others want, then you give the world something new. And Kanye West also says that, that I don't care about what my audience thinks, I just do what I want to do, and in that way they like it. So I think it's a mix of both: strategy because you want to be winning every single time, you also need to study what has worked for you, but also you just need to do things your way, because even people don't know what they like and why they like it. So you might as well just take a chance and it might do wonders for you. Host: Do you think that algorithm actually drives your content, basically when you study algorithm and create content, or how does it work? Do you happen to like check whether these kind of content works on the Instagram platform and then you create, or how do you research on your topics before posting something? Simridhi Makhija: So the thing is, Instagram treats every reel as a one-shot reel. So it doesn't care how your earlier reels have performed. If your reel that you're posting in that moment has real substance to it, it'll show to people. And that's your superpower, you know? So then what I try to do is that I try to be most myself and I try to say my truth, because in a world wherein everybody is trying to fool you, everybody's trying to get something out of you, I just want to be myself. I just want to again retard-max and see where the algorithm takes it. And my best-performing reels have been the ones wherein I have been the most genuine. And by the way, I have also tried to be fake and tried to engineer it, because everybody does that, but that hasn't worked for me, and I think yeah, that's the way to go about it. Host: When it comes to like, see, you are a person who just in bio you mentioned that figuring out life in 20s, right? So a lot of Gen Zs are there. Raj Shamani and Viraj Seth, both of them support a lot to Gen Z people. Few feel they're very lazy and few feel they're very much talented, but they don't have the right environment or the company that actually takes work from them. What do you think, since you have dated a few people here and you have gone through a lot of networking and people here, also interacted with a lot of content creators, how can we handle them? Simridhi Makhija: So I think I have a hot take on that. Being a Gen Z myself, I don't like the culture that's going on with the Gen Z. And the reason is that everybody's so entitled, so entitled, that I am not going to work after 7:00 PM, I'm not going to take the call, I'm going to leave the meeting, and I'm going to tell the boss that you know what, I am off and you don't get to tell me what to do. But the thing is, the only way to mastery is being humble, putting your head down, and putting in the work. So where this entitlement is coming from is something that I don't understand amongst Gen Z, being a Gen Z myself. That's just the honest truth. I feel like if you want to be the best in your game, you have to be humble and respect people who are above you, both in terms of experience and in terms of age. But if you move through the world thinking that the world will give you things, then thank you for thinking that, because you're reducing my competition. But that's not the way that it works, that's the only thing I'll say. But having said that, if your aim in life is to make a simple living, then great, you can, you know, give yourself this lie that this is how the world is supposed to be. But just know that the people who are really going for the things that they want do not care about boundaries, do not care about how late they are working, they're just going for it. Host: To outperform others, you have to outperform yourself first of all. Simridhi Makhija: 100%. And then you have to also remove all the propaganda that social media has taught you that you're good enough and then you're the best and then you need to have boundaries and don't let anybody tell you that you're not good enough. Please let everybody tell you that you're not good enough, because a 21-year-old is not good enough. Host: Correct. That's pretty interesting. And also happened to see like a lot of Gen Zs are very much interested on dating, right, but a lot of them end up being single, and a lot of reels that you have posted has been shared by Gen Zs is what I feel. So why is that gap? Since they are a generation which has everything, everything very accessible, still they end up being single. Why do you think so? Simridhi Makhija: We started off this podcast by saying that, you know, we are not wired to lead the life that we are leading, and I'm so shocked that nobody even talks about it, nobody cares. But we are literally watching the best people in the world all day, every day, and we are comparing our lives with them. But the truth of the matter is that biologically speaking, you are only supposed to know three guys who were in your neighborhood, and you were only supposed to marry one of them, right? But now you have matches from across the world if you just change the geography in your dating app, and that is messing things up. Because you want the ultra best for yourself, but maybe you're not the ultra best yourself. But social media is feeding that propaganda that no, you should go for the best. So that realism has completely ended, and that is exactly where the gap is. So this is what I believe. I think if you want to reduce that gap, you need to know exactly what you want in life, exactly what you want from a partner, and also have realistic expectations. I think that is something that's that the new generation is not realizing. Because even somebody who is not that great in terms of career, let's say, wants a partner who's the CEO of a unicorn, you know, but that just doesn't work like that. So I think realism is something that will solve not just your dating life, but honestly your professional life as well. Host: A lot of girls post the dating screenshots of the guys they do or the guys also do vice versa. And then they complain about a few things that they have done in that part, right? It should be a private scene, is what I feel, because people trust you and text you in the dating apps. Do you think it's actually you should do that, or how does it work? Simridhi Makhija: I think you should do that without naming the person. I'll tell you exactly why, because we need to know what's happening in the dating world. Like I would rather know what a guy sitting in Bangalore is saying to a girl he just met. Like is he crossing his line? Is he saying something completely out of bounds? I would rather know that, instead of just trusting the world and thinking that they are the best and they are okay. No, I should know through those screenshots so that I can be more wary, is my logic. So so far as you're not maligning anybody, I think it's fine. Host: In a reel, Viraj told that don't take dating advice from men. That kind of content won't work is what he told. And when happened to see your content, you also give some dating advice and that goes viral. Okay, so why people tend to take dating advice from girls rather than boys and they don't trust boys, why? Simridhi Makhija: Because the world knows that men will go for anything and women have standards, so like they'll pick and choose. Obviously that's not true, like obviously men have their own criteria, I'm sure.
